items.title: A Fake \"You're Invited\" Email Is the New Way In
items.summary: Scammers are breaking into regular email accounts and sending fake invitations — a birthday party, a fundraiser, a wedding — from someone you actually know. Click "view the invitation" and it asks you to sign in with Google, Apple, or Microsoft; that login screen is fake, and the password you type goes straight to the crooks. A real invitation never asks you to log in just to see it. I tell folks to check with the sender by a quick call first.

items.title: Firefox just got a cleaner new look that can tuck your tabs down the left side — update free at firefox.com
items.summary: Open Firefox, click the Menu button (the three lines in the top-right corner), then Help, then About Firefox — it checks for the new version and installs it for you in about two minutes. Don't have Firefox yet? Go to firefox.com and click Download; it's free and it's made by Mozilla.

items.title: Someone using your Google account? Google's free Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup shows every device signed in
items.summary: Open myaccount.google.com/security-checkup in your browser, sign in with your Google account, and follow the short list it shows you. It reviews the devices signed in to your account, the apps that have access to it, and any password it thinks is weak or reused — and it walks you through fixing each one. No download, no cost, about two minutes.

items.title: A 'New Plastic Medicare Card' in the Mail Is a Scam
items.summary: An official-looking plastic Medicare card is landing in mailboxes, with a phone number to "activate" your new benefits — and that call is the whole scam. Real Medicare cards are paper, and nobody from Medicare will ever call, text, or email asking for your Medicare, Social Security, or bank number. Don't ring a number printed on the letter — type medicare.gov into your browser yourself, or use 800-633-4227, the number I check before I trust it. Already shared it? Report it at ftc.gov.

items.title: Is your email in a data breach? Check free in seconds at haveibeenpwned.com and turn on alerts so a scammer never gets there first
items.summary: Open haveibeenpwned.com in your browser, type your email address in the box, and click the button. It is free, it takes about ten seconds, and you do not have to create an account or hand over a password. Then scroll down the page and click Notify me, so it sends you an email the day your address shows up in a future leak.

items.title: Tired of ads following you everywhere? Brave is the free browser at brave.com that blocks them by itself — nothing to add, nothing to pay
items.summary: Go to brave.com and click the Download button, install it, and then use it exactly like your current browser. Brave blocks ads and the trackers that follow you from site to site on its own, the moment you install it. You do not add anything, you do not change any settings, and you never pay a cent.

items.title: If Someone Wants You to Pay With Gift Cards, It's a Scam
items.summary: Police put out a fresh warning this week that gift-card scams are going after older adults and draining savings. Here is a rule that never fails: no real bank, sheriff's office, insurance company, or store will ever ask you to pay a bill with gift cards. Once you read the numbers off the back, the money is gone and there is no refund. If a caller keeps you on the line and pushes you to go buy cards, hang up — I've never once seen a real bill that worked that way.

items.title: Cannot open a file someone emailed you? 7-Zip is the free file opener at 7-zip.org that unpacks ZIP and RAR files — no account, no ads, nothing to pay
items.summary: Go to 7-zip.org and click the big Download link for Windows near the top of the page, install it, and you are done. From then on, right-click any ZIP or RAR file and choose 7-Zip, then Extract Here. The contents appear right next to the file, free, forever.

items.title: Your family pictures live in one place only — Windows File History keeps an automatic second copy on a $60 portable drive from Walmart; press Start, type File History, and click Turn on
items.summary: Buy a portable drive — Seagate, Western Digital, and Toshiba all make good ones, and they run about $60 at Walmart or Best Buy — then plug it into the computer with the cord that comes in the box. Press the Start button, type File History, open it, and click Turn on. From then on, Windows copies your Documents, Pictures, and Desktop onto that drive every hour, by itself, without you clicking anything ever again.

items.title: Microsoft Pulled the Update That Switched Off Word and Excel
items.summary: Microsoft pulled a faulty update that switched off Word and Excel on home computers — people opened a document and were told their software was unlicensed, or found it gone. One repair shop had five customers hit within ten minutes, and I've had calls here too. Don't pay to fix it, and be wary of any message offering to do it for you — that's where the scam starts. Open Word or Excel, click Reactivate, and sign in with the account you normally use; if it's gone, reinstall the copy you bought.

items.title: Stop renting Microsoft Office — LibreOffice is the free office suite at libreoffice.org that opens Word, Excel and PowerPoint files and never sends your documents to AI
items.summary: Download LibreOffice free from libreoffice.org, install it, and it opens your Word, Excel and PowerPoint files just like the paid versions. There is no subscription, no account, and no AI reading your documents — it works completely on your own computer, even offline.

items.title: Can't hear the TV or a video on your computer? Windows 11's free Live Captions types out the words — turn it on with Windows key + Ctrl + L
items.summary: On a Windows 11 computer, press the Windows key, Ctrl, and L at the same time to turn on Live Captions, or open Settings > Accessibility > Captions and flip the Live captions switch. It is free and built in, and it shows on-screen text for any sound your computer plays — a video, a call, or a DVD.
